original_question: For the focusing nonlinear Schrodinger equation on the half-line with oscillatory boundary forcing u(0,t) = e^{i w t}, can one show that as w decreases toward 0 the boundary drive excites k-gap solutions of periodic NLS?
target_in_paper: Problem 5, especially the sentence stating the expected low-frequency behavior for the half-line focusing NLS IBVP: Deift writes that one expects “similar behavior for focusing NLS, with k-gap solutions of periodic NLS emerging from the driver e^{iwt} as w ↓ 0,” immediately after formulating the stand-out open problem of determining the long-time behavior of the solution with u(x,0)=f(x) and u(0,t)=e^{iwt}. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2017/016/sigma17-016.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the right equation family (focusing NLS), the half-line setting, the oscillatory Dirichlet boundary forcing u(0,t)=e^{iwt}, and the specific phenomenon the paper highlights in this context: the expected emergence of k-gap solutions of periodic NLS as the driving frequency tends to 0. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2017/016/sigma17-016.pdf))
missing_details: The paper frames this inside a broader long-time asymptotic problem: the official open problem is to determine the behavior of u(x,t) as t→∞, not only to assert a low-frequency excitation mechanism. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2017/016/sigma17-016.pdf))
The exact PDE should be stated: i u_t = u_xx + 2|u|^2 u. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2017/016/sigma17-016.pdf))
The spatial-temporal domain is part of the formulation: x≥0 and t≥0. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2017/016/sigma17-016.pdf))

The official formulation includes prescribed initial data u(x,0)=f(x) for x≥0; your draft omits the initial condition altogether. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2017/016/sigma17-016.pdf))
The boundary forcing is specifically Dirichlet data u(0,t)=e^{iwt} for t≥0 with parameter w∈R. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2017/016/sigma17-016.pdf))

The paper does not specify explicit regularity, decay, or compatibility assumptions on f in this informal open-problem statement, so a faithful rewrite should not invent extra hypotheses. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2017/016/sigma17-016.pdf))

The k-gap claim is presented as expected phenomenology motivated by the Toda-lattice analogy, not as a formally quantified conjecture with explicit threshold frequencies, a prescribed law k=k(w), or a statement for each fixed k. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2017/016/sigma17-016.pdf))

Nearby context records only partial results in the opposite regime w→∞, which helps delimit what the paper treats as known versus open. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2017/016/sigma17-016.pdf))
refined_question: For the half-line initial-boundary value problem for the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation i u_t = u_xx + 2|u|^2 u on x≥0, t≥0, with prescribed initial data u(x,0)=f(x) for x≥0 and Dirichlet boundary forcing u(0,t)=e^{iwt} for t≥0, w∈R, determine the long-time asymptotic behavior of u(x,t) as t→∞; in particular, can one justify the expected low-frequency scenario that, as w↓0, finite-gap (k-gap) solutions of periodic NLS emerge from the boundary driver e^{iwt}? ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2017/016/sigma17-016.pdf))
justification: The draft is targeting the specific expectation in Problem 5 rather than a different open problem in the paper. Deift first singles out the open problem of computing the long-time behavior of the half-line focusing NLS solution with given initial data u(x,0)=f(x) and oscillatory boundary data u(0,t)=e^{iwt}, w∈R. He then introduces the Toda-lattice analogy and states the anticipated NLS analogue: as the driving frequency decreases, k-gap solutions of periodic NLS should emerge from the boundary driver as w↓0. Your draft captures that anticipated low-frequency phenomenon, but it leaves implicit the PDE itself, the initial condition, the domain x≥0, t≥0, and the fact that the paper places the question inside a t→∞ asymptotic-analysis problem rather than as an isolated yes/no conjecture. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2017/016/sigma17-016.pdf))
